provenance.other: “had all things common” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 2:44 and Acts 4:32, both describing the Jerusalem church. “of one heart and of one soul” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:32, and 4 Nephi 1:15 supplies its equivalent — one love dwelling in the hearts of the people.
provenance.significance: The community of goods is not the only thing 4 Nephi takes from Acts 4. Acts 4:32-37 ends by naming Barnabas, who sold a field and laid the whole price at the apostles' feet; Acts 5:1-2 opens with Ananias, who kept back part of the price and died for it. 3 Nephi 26 reached for this passage as its closing image and the catalogue noted there that its source's next sentence is about withholding. 4 Nephi is the book in which the withholding actually happens: at 1:25 'they did have their goods and their substance no more common among them', and the two hundred years of Acts 4 end in the sentence that undoes it. Read metaleptically, the whole apostasy of 4 Nephi is Acts 5:1 arriving late.

1:3.note: 'And they had all things common among them, therefore there were not rich and poor, bond and free, but they were all made free.' The four-word clause has two homes in the King James Bible and both are Acts's portrait of the Jerusalem church, which this chapter has been assembling since its first verse: baptism in the name of Jesus and the gift of the Holy Ghost at 1:1 (Acts 2:38), the whole people converted at 1:2 (Acts 2:47), all things common at 1:3, continuance in prayer and in meeting together at 1:12 (Acts 2:42, 2:46). The borrowing is not a phrase but a chapter. The link is adjudicated in full at 3 Nephi 26:19, where the same clause enters the corpus; this row records it re-entering in Mormon's own book, where it becomes the premise of two hundred years of narrative rather than a closing image. Note that the four-term abolition — rich and poor, bond and free — is not Acts's: “bond and free” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, and the pairing of wealth with legal status belongs to Galatians 3:28 and Revelation 13:16 (see the exclusion register at this verse).
1:3.text: And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.

provenance.other: “heavenly gift” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 6:4. The construction the Book of Mormon actually writes, partakers of the heavenly gift, is a splice: “partakers of the heavenly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 3:1, where the noun is 'calling'. Hebrews 6:4 has both halves but distributes them — tasted of the heavenly gift, made partakers of the Holy Ghost — and 4 Nephi 1:1 has just used the second half, 'they did also receive the Holy Ghost'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's thesis statement and it is planted at the top. Hebrews 6:4-6 is the King James Bible's hardest sentence about apostasy: those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and shall fall away — 'it is impossible ... to renew them again unto repentance.' 4 Nephi describes a people who receive exactly those three things in its first three verses and then spends forty-six verses falling away from them. The metalepsis is structural rather than local: recover Hebrews 6 and the golden age is being narrated in the vocabulary of the one passage that says a golden age of this kind cannot be recovered. The companion passage, Hebrews 10:26 on sinning wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth, arrives at 4 Nephi 1:38 to close the arc.

1:3.note: 'And partakers of the Heavenly gift.' The noun is a King James singleton and the phrase around it is built from the two Hebrews verses that use 'partakers of the heavenly'. What makes the borrowing more than a phrase is that 4 Nephi 1:1-3 reproduces Hebrews 6:4's whole triad in order — enlightenment through the disciples' preaching, the Holy Ghost received (1:1), the heavenly gift partaken (1:3) — and that the corpus has used this verse before for precisely the apostasy it introduces: Alma 24:30 argues from 'once enlightened' and 'fall away' that a people who have known and then fallen become more hardened than if they had never known. 4 Nephi is that argument as narrative.
1:3.text: For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

provenance.route: Matthew 15:31 + Matthew 11:5 + Mark 7:37 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Three King James singletons meet in one clause. “the lame to walk” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 15:31; “receive their sight” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 11:5; “the deaf to hear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 7:37. The Book of Mormon's syntax is Matthew 15:31's throughout — the infinitive series governed by a verb of causing — and into it are set the one KJV phrase for a blind man's cure and the one KJV phrase for a deaf man's.
provenance.significance: Matthew 11:5 is Jesus's answer to John the Baptist's question, 'Art thou he that should come?', and it is an answer made of Isaiah 35:5-6: the works are offered as the credential of the Messiah. Matthew 15:31 is the crowd's reaction — 'and they glorified the God of Israel'. Recover both and the verse is doing something the Book of Mormon does not say aloud: the disciples' miracles are described in the exact words by which Jesus proved he was the Christ, and the verse ends by insisting that 'in nothing did they work miracles save it were in the name of Jesus'. The credential is transferred and the transfer is immediately qualified.

1:5.note: 'They did heal the sick, and raise the dead, and cause the lame to walk, and the blind to receive their sight, and the deaf to hear.' The eight-word run 'the lame to walk, and the blind to' is Matthew 15:31's, whose own list runs 'the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see'. Where Matthew 15:31 has 'to see', 4 Nephi has 'to receive their sight', which is Matthew 11:5's phrase and nobody else's; where neither Matthew has the deaf as an infinitive, 4 Nephi has 'the deaf to hear', which is Mark 7:37's phrase and nobody else's. So this is not one verse borrowed but three fused, with a fourth element — raising the dead — supplied from Matthew 11:5's 'the dead are raised up'. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; catalogued as an allusion because no single verse is reproduced whole.
1:5.text: Insomuch that the multitude wondered, when they saw the dumb to speak, the maimed to be whole, the lame to walk, and the blind to see: and they glorified the God of Israel.

provenance.other: “given in marriage” occurs in exactly five KJV verses: Matthew 22:30, Mark 12:25, Luke 17:27, Luke 20:34 and Luke 20:35. Luke 17:27 is the only one with the Book of Mormon's passive-plus-conjunction form, 'they married ... they were given in marriage'; the rest all pair 'marry' with 'are given'. The nearest single-verse formula, “marrying and giving in marriage”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 24:38, and is not the form used here.
provenance.significance: This is the finding, and it costs the verse its innocence. In the King James Bible marrying and being given in marriage is never a blessing. Two of its five occurrences are the resurrection debate, where it is the thing that does not happen in the world to come; the other three are the days of Noe — 'they did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all.' It is the King James idiom for ordinary life going on in complete ignorance of what is about to happen. 4 Nephi 1:11 is the single sentence of domestic blessing in the golden age, and it is worded in the one biblical formula for a generation with two hundred years left.

1:11.note: 'And they were married, and given in marriage, and were blessed according to the multitude of the promises which the Lord had made unto them.' Filed as an echo at moderate because the phrase has five King James homes and any of them could supply it; a writer describing marriages has few other English idioms available. What lifts it above coincidence is the form — Luke 17:27's passive, not the resurrection chapters' — and the fact that the verse's second half insists on the promises, which is exactly the security Luke 17:26-30 describes the antediluvians and the Sodomites as having.
1:11.whyNot: 'Given in marriage' is common enough in the KJV that no source is demonstrable, and the Book of Mormon may simply be reaching for the one biblical way of saying that people married. The metaleptic reading in provenance is ours and depends on the reader granting that a writer steeped in the KJV would hear Noe behind the phrase; a reader who declines that hears nothing but a wedding.
1:11.text: They did eat, they drank, they married wives, they were given in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark, and the flood came, and destroyed them all.

provenance.other: “walk any more after” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 3:17, and so does the longer run “any more after the”. Not quoted anywhere in the New Testament, so no mediation test is available; the borrowing is from the Old Testament KJV directly.
provenance.significance: Jeremiah 3:16-17 is the King James Bible's one promise that the machinery of Israel's worship will simply cease to be missed: 'they shall say no more, The ark of the covenant of the LORD: neither shall it come to mind: neither shall they remember it; neither shall they visit it; neither shall that be done any more. At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the LORD, and all the nations shall be gathered unto it.' 4 Nephi 1:12 is the abolition of the law of Moses, and it borrows its verb from the one prophetic sentence in which a cultus is retired without being mourned. The gathering half of Jeremiah 3:17 then arrives five verses later at 4 Nephi 1:17, where the -ites are dissolved into one — which is why this row and the John 11:52 row belong read together.

1:12.note: 'And they did not walk any more after the performances and ordinances of the law of Moses.' Five contiguous words from a King James singleton, and the singleton is the right one: Jeremiah 3:17's 'neither shall they walk any more after the imagination of their evil heart' is the clause that follows the promise that the ark will not be remembered. The Book of Mormon substitutes the law of Moses for the imagination of the evil heart, which is a substitution with a doctrine in it — the thing walked after and now abandoned is not idolatry but the divinely given cultus itself. Neither 'performances' nor 'ordinances of the law' occurs in the KJV at all, so the Book of Mormon's own vocabulary supplies the object and Jeremiah supplies the frame.
1:12.text: At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the LORD; and all the nations shall be gathered unto it, to the name of the LORD, to Jerusalem: neither shall they walk any more after the imagination of their evil heart.

provenance.other: “continued stedfastly” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:42, and “assembling of ourselves together” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:25 — but the Book of Mormon reproduces neither string, writing 'continuing' and 'meeting together oft'. The contact is with the shape of Acts 2:42-46, not with its wording.
provenance.significance: Acts 2:42 lists four things the first church continued in: the apostles' doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers. 4 Nephi 1:12 lists three: fasting and prayer, meeting together oft, and hearing the word of the Lord. What has dropped out is the breaking of bread — which 3 Nephi 26:13 had already supplied, and which the sacrament chapters of 3 Nephi 18 had established at length. The list is Acts's minus what this corpus has already narrated.

1:12.note: 'Continuing in fasting and prayer, and in meeting together oft, both to pray and to hear the word of the Lord.' No King James verse is reproduced here and none is claimed; what is claimed is that the sentence completes an Acts 2 pattern the chapter has been running since 1:1 — baptism and the Holy Ghost (Acts 2:38), the whole people converted (Acts 2:47), all things common (Acts 2:44, adjudicated at 1:3), and now continuance in prayer and assembly (Acts 2:42, 2:46). Filed at moderate and as a paraphrase for that reason: the argument is cumulative and the individual verse would not carry it alone. Hebrews 10:25 is recorded as a composite because it is the KJV's one sentence about not forsaking the assembly, but the Book of Mormon's 'meeting together oft' shares no word with it beyond 'together'.
1:12.text: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

provenance.other: “the love of God” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses, which on its own settles nothing. The verb is what settles it: “dwelleth the love of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:17. Of the twelve, only this one has the love of God dwelling in anybody; Romans 5:5 sheds it abroad in the heart and 2 Thessalonians 3:5 directs the heart into it.
provenance.significance: 1 John 3:17 asks its question about a specific man: 'whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?' The test John applies to the indwelling of the love of God is whether a man with goods shares them with a brother in need. 4 Nephi has just said, at 1:3, that these people had all things common; it now says that there was no contention because the love of God dwelt in their hearts. Ten verses later the goods stop being common (1:25) and the people divide into classes (1:26). John's verse supplies both the term for the golden age and the diagnostic by which its ending is recognised, and the Book of Mormon lets the second half arrive without comment.

1:15.note: 'And it came to pass that there was no contention in the land, because of the love of God which did dwell in the hearts of the people.' The phrase 'the love of God' is far too common in the KJV to identify a source, and the machine's proposal here was Romans 8:39. The verb decides it: nowhere in the King James Bible does the love of God dwell in anyone except at 1 John 3:17, and there the whole point of the sentence is that shared goods are the proof of the indwelling. Filed at moderate rather than high because the Book of Mormon reverses the question into a statement and shares only three words plus the verb; the case rests on the collocation and on the fact that 1 John 3:17's condition is 4 Nephi's situation exactly.
1:15.text: But whoso hath this world’s good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?

provenance.other: Three plurals decide it. “envyings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Corinthians 12:20 and Galatians 5:21; “strifes” occurs in exactly four; “tumults” occurs in exactly three. The one verse carrying all three is 2 Corinthians 12:20, and it carries them in the Book of Mormon's order — envyings, then strifes, then tumults. 'Lasciviousness' then comes from the next verse, 2 Corinthians 12:21, which is where Paul's list of what he fears to find continues.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a fear about a church he is coming back to: 'lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults.' 4 Nephi 1:16 takes that catalogue and negates it item by item — 'there were no envyings, nor strifes, nor tumults' — and concludes that 'surely there could not be a happier people among all the people which had been created by the hand of God'. The happiest people in the Book of Mormon are defined by the absence of the vices Paul expected to find at Corinth. Read forward, the same list is what Helaman 13:22 found present in the Nephites a century earlier and what 4 Nephi 1:24-26 will find present again; the corpus uses 2 Corinthians 12:20 as its standing inventory of what a church looks like when it goes wrong.

1:16.note: 'And there were no envyings, nor strifes, nor tumults, nor whoredoms, nor lyings, nor murders, nor no manner of lasciviousness.' Three of the seven items are rare King James plurals and exactly one KJV verse holds all three, in this order. The Book of Mormon's remaining four are supplied from the surrounding verses and from the other vice catalogue: 'lasciviousness' from 2 Corinthians 12:21, 'murders' from Galatians 5:21 (which also has 'envyings'), and 'whoredoms' and 'lyings' from its own idiom. The catalogue has been here before — Helaman 13:22 draws on the same verse for swelling, envyings and strifes — but this is the first time the list is negated rather than charged, and the negation is what makes it worth a full row rather than a cross-reference. Note the 1830 reading 'nor no manner of lasciviousness', a double negative the 1920 edition removed by changing 'no' to 'any'.
1:16.text: For I fear, lest, when I come, I shall not find you such as I would, and that I shall be found unto you such as ye would not: lest there be debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults:

provenance.other: “in one the children of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 11:52. Galatians 3:28's 'ye are all one in Christ Jesus' is the obvious rival for the idea and shares no run at all; “bond nor free” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11, and the Book of Mormon's own 'bond and free' at 1:3 occurs in exactly zero.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's best borrowing and its force is entirely metaleptic. John 11:52 is the evangelist's gloss on Caiaphas: having reported that the high priest said it was expedient that one man should die for the people, John adds that he spake not of himself but prophesied, 'and not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.' The Book of Mormon has used the first half of that saying already, at 1 Nephi 4:13, where Caiaphas's arithmetic justifies the killing of Laban. Six hundred years later in the narrative, the second half arrives as its answer: the scattered children are gathered, there are no Lamanites nor any manner of -ites, and 'they were in one, the children of Christ'. One book's opening act of violence is licensed by John 11:50 and its one moment of realised unity is worded from John 11:52. Neither text says this. The two links together say it.

1:17.note: 'But they were in one, the children of Christ, and heirs to the kingdom of God.' Five contiguous words from a King James singleton, with the one substitution that matters: John's 'children of God' becomes 'children of Christ'. The rest of the verse dissolves precisely the categories John 11:52 says the gathering will overcome — nation and dispersion — and does it by abolishing the -ites, which is this corpus's own name for its divisions. The rival source for the sentiment, Galatians 3:28, shares the thought and not one distinctive word, and is recorded as a composite rather than an alternative for that reason. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations.
1:17.text: And not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.

provenance.other: “heirs of the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 2:5. The Book of Mormon's 1830 reading is 'heirs to the kingdom of God', with James's genitive replaced by a dative and 'of God' supplied — a change of preposition, not of phrase.
provenance.significance: James 2:5 asks whether God has not chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith, to be heirs of the kingdom, and James 2:6 — which 2 Nephi 9:30 has already used — goes on to condemn those who despise the poor. 4 Nephi 1:3 has just abolished the distinction: 'there were not rich and poor'. So the verse that makes poverty the qualification for the inheritance is being applied to a people among whom poverty no longer exists, and the abolition of the category is what makes them heirs rather than their place within it. James's economics are not contradicted; they are made unnecessary, which is a stranger result and a more interesting one.

1:17.note: 'And heirs to the kingdom of God.' A King James singleton, and the one KJV verse that makes anyone an heir of the kingdom does it on an economic condition this chapter has spent fourteen verses removing. Filed at moderate rather than high because the phrase is short, because 'heirs' and 'kingdom of God' are separately common, and because Galatians 3:29 and Titus 3:7 give the corpus other inheritance idioms it uses elsewhere; what argues for James specifically is the singleton plus the fact that the corpus has been in James 2 before, at 2 Nephi 9:30.
1:17.text: Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him?

provenance.other: “costly array” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 2:9; the Book of Mormon's own “costly apparel” occurs in exactly zero, but 'apparel' is 1 Timothy 2:9's noun as well ('modest apparel'). “pearls” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, and 1 Timothy 2:9 is the only one that puts pearls and costliness in a list of what not to wear.
provenance.significance: The apostasy of 4 Nephi begins in a wardrobe. 1 Timothy 2:9-10 is not a passage about luxury in general but about what women wear to church — 'not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.' The next thing 4 Nephi records is that they began to build up churches unto themselves (1:26) and that there were churches which professed to know the Christ (1:27). 'Professing godliness' is the phrase 1 Timothy attaches to the alternative; 'professed to know the Christ' is what 4 Nephi 1:27 says of the churches that got the wardrobe instead. Recover 1 Timothy 2:9's own next clause and the chapter's sequence — costly apparel, then churches, then profession — is already there.

1:24.note: 'Those which were lifted up in pride, such as the wearing of costly apparel, and all manner of fine pearls, and of the fine things of the world.' The pride-of-heart formula is the Book of Mormon's own and is covered by the standing exclusion filed at 3 Nephi 6:10; what is borrowed is the wardrobe. Jacob 2:13 already drew 'costliness of your apparel' from this verse, and the catalogue's argument for it is made there. This row is written rather than cross-referenced because 4 Nephi adds the pearls, and pearls and costly array occur together in exactly one KJV verse — so the second use is closer to the source than the first was. It is also the hinge of the book: this is the sentence in which two hundred years of peace end.
1:24.text: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;

provenance.other: “profess that they know” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Titus 1:16. The rival formula for the same idea, “form of godliness”, occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 3:5, and shares no wording with 4 Nephi 1:27 at all; it is recorded as a composite because the Book of Mormon's 'deny the more parts of his gospel' is nearer 2 Timothy's 'denying the power thereof' than to Titus's 'in works they deny him'.
provenance.significance: Titus 1:16 is describing not apostates in general but a specific failure of church officers: the verses before it are Paul's instructions for ordaining elders, and the verses after are about teaching what becomes sound doctrine. 4 Nephi 1:27's own second half is about administration — 'did administer that which was sacred unto him to whom it had been forbidden, because of unworthiness'. So the source verse and the borrowing verse are both about ordained men handling holy things they have disqualified themselves from. The profession-and-denial formula arrives with its ecclesiastical setting attached, and 4 Nephi uses that setting rather than discarding it.

1:27.note: 'There were churches which professed to know the Christ, and yet they did deny the more parts of his gospel.' A King James singleton supplies the first half — 'They profess that they know God' — and the second half reproduces its adversative: 'but in works they deny him'. The Book of Mormon substitutes Christ for God and the gospel's parts for the works, keeping the sentence's shape intact. This is the fullest of the chapter's apostasy borrowings and it sits at the exact point where the many churches appear; every element of Titus 1:16's clause is present and only its nouns are changed.
1:27.text: They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate.

provenance.route: John 7:1 (+ John 12:37) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “sought to kill him” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 4:24 (the LORD meeting Moses in the inn) and John 7:1 — and John 7:1 is the only one in which the Jews are the subject, which is what 4 Nephi names. For the first half of the verse, “so many miracles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “yet they believed not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are John 12:37.
provenance.significance: 4 Nephi 1:31 makes its own comparison out loud — the people sought to kill the disciples 'even as the Jews at Jerusalem sought to kill Jesus' — which is unusual: most of this catalogue's links are borrowings the text does not acknowledge. What the text does not say is that it has also borrowed the sentence structure of the comparison. John 12:37 stands at the exact hinge of the Fourth Gospel, closing the book of signs: he had done so many miracles before them, yet they believed not. 4 Nephi 1:31 stands at the same hinge in its own book, closing the account of the disciples' miracles and opening the account of the persecution. The chapter is not merely comparing its people to the Jews at Jerusalem; it is placing its own narrative turn where John placed his.

1:31.note: 'Nevertheless, and notwithstanding all these miracles the people did harden their hearts, and did seek to kill them, even as the Jews at Jerusalem sought to kill Jesus, according to his word.' The final clause is John 7:1's, minus one word — 'because the Jews sought to kill him' — and John 7:1 adds the detail 4 Nephi supplies as 'at Jerusalem', since its point is that Jesus would not walk in Jewry. The concessive first half is John 12:37's proposition in the Book of Mormon's idiom. The middle clause, 'did harden their hearts', looks like a third contact with John 12:40, whose 'hardened their heart' is a KJV singleton — but the Book of Mormon's plural form matches Joshua 11:20 and is a standing formula in this corpus, so no weight is put on it; see the exclusion register at this verse. Mediation is direct-NT on John 7:1's own account, and the John 12:40 half of the case is deliberately left undecided.
1:31.text: After these things Jesus walked in Galilee: for he would not walk in Jewry, because the Jews sought to kill him.

provenance.route: Matthew 13:42 (+ Daniel 3) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “furnace of fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 13:42 and Matthew 13:50, which are the same formula repeated within one chapter. “cast them into a furnace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:42. Daniel 3, which supplies the episode, never uses the phrase: its furnace is always 'the burning fiery furnace'.
provenance.significance: The borrowing is an inversion and the inversion is the point. In Matthew 13:41-42 the Son of man sends forth his angels to gather out of his kingdom 'them which do iniquity', and shall cast them into a furnace of fire. In 4 Nephi 1:32 it is the men who do iniquity who do the casting, and the ones cast in come forth receiving no harm. Matthew's phrase for the final punishment of the wicked has been handed to the wicked as a method, and it fails. That 4 Nephi 1:34 then describes the persecutors as those who 'do all manner of iniquity' — where “them which do iniquity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:41, the verse immediately before — suggests the whole pericope, not the phrase, is in view.

1:32.note: 'And they did cast them into furnaces of fire, and they came forth receiving no harm.' The narrative is Daniel 3's — three men thrown into a furnace by a persecuting power and coming out untouched — and 3 Nephi 28:21 has already told it once, where the catalogue filed it as figural on the grounds that there was no verbal contact at all. The retelling here acquires the contact: 'cast them into a furnace of fire' is Matthew 13:42 word for word except that 4 Nephi pluralises the furnaces, and Daniel's own KJV wording ('the burning fiery furnace', 'came forth of the midst of the fire') is nowhere in the sentence. That is a real finding about the corpus rather than about this verse: between 3 Nephi 28 and 4 Nephi 1 the same episode is re-narrated and the wording moves toward the King James Bible, not away from it.
1:32.text: And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth.

provenance.other: “shall play” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Samuel 16:16 (David on the harp) and Isaiah 11:8, and only Isaiah's has a child playing among dangerous animals. The lamb comes from Isaiah 11:6. The passage is not quoted in the New Testament — Romans 15:12 takes Isaiah 11:10, not 11:6-8 — so no mediation test is available.
provenance.significance: The peaceable kingdom has changed hands. 2 Nephi 21 transcribes Isaiah 11 whole as prophecy and 2 Nephi 30:14 applies it to a future millennium; 4 Nephi 1:33 has just lost the two-hundred-year peace that came nearest to it. What survives of Isaiah's vision at this point in the narrative is one simile, attached to three men being thrown to beasts by their neighbours. The image of the child at play with the deadly animal is now a description of martyrdom rather than of a restored creation.

1:33.note: 'They did play with the wild beasts even as a child with a lamb.' The full argument for this compression of Isaiah 11:6-8 is made at 3 Nephi 28:22, where the same sentence is told the first time and reads 'as a child with a suckling lamb'; this row records the borrowing re-entering in Mormon's own book rather than restating it. Filed at moderate for the same reason it was there: four words of contact across two Isaiah verses, in a simile the Book of Mormon could have reached without a source.
1:33.text: And the sucking child shall play on the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the cockatrice’ den.

provenance.other: “reviled not again” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Peter 2:23, and it is the King James Bible's only instance of the construction the Book of Mormon uses here — a verb of injury, negated, plus 'again', to mean a refusal to retaliate in kind. “smite him again” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses.
provenance.significance: 1 Peter 2:21-23 is the passage that makes non-retaliation an imitation: 'Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps ... who, when he was reviled, reviled not again.' 4 Nephi 1:34 calls the sufferers 'the people of Jesus' twice in one sentence — the only place in the chapter it uses that name — and then describes them doing what 1 Peter says Christ did. The name and the behaviour arrive together. Note also that 4 Nephi 1:31 has just compared their persecutors to the Jews at Jerusalem who sought to kill Jesus; the two verses complete the imitation from both ends.

1:34.note: 'And they did smite upon the people of Jesus; but the people of Jesus did not smite again.' The doctrine is the Sermon's — turn the other cheek — and this corpus has it in its own scripture at 3 Nephi 12:39, delivered by Jesus to these people's ancestors, which is the proximate warrant for the behaviour. But the King James Bible's way of saying that someone declined to return an injury is 1 Peter 2:23's, and 'did not smite again' is that construction with the verb changed. Filed at moderate: the shared vocabulary is one word plus a syntactic pattern, and a writer could reach 'did not smite again' without a source. What argues for it is the pattern's rarity and the doubled 'people of Jesus'. Flagged for a convention gap: the mediation field has no value for a New Testament source reaching a verse through an earlier Book of Mormon quotation, so this is recorded as direct-NT with 3 Nephi 12:39 in recurrenceRefs.
1:34.text: Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:

provenance.other: “wilfully” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 10:26. The 1830 spelling is the King James spelling, with one l; modern editions print 'wilfully' still, but the word's single King James home is worth naming because the Book of Mormon uses it exactly where Hebrews does — of sin committed after knowledge, as distinct from sin committed in ignorance.
provenance.significance: This verse and 4 Nephi 1:3 are the two ends of one argument. Hebrews has two passages on apostasy after enlightenment: 6:4-6, on those who have tasted the heavenly gift and fallen away, and 10:26, on those who sin wilfully after receiving the knowledge of the truth. 4 Nephi opens its golden age with the vocabulary of the first and closes its account of the division with the adverb of the second, and it uses the distinction Hebrews draws to make a distinction of its own: those who 'did not dwindle in unbelief, but did wilfully rebel'. Hebrews 10:26's consequence — 'there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins' — is not quoted, but it is the reason the Lamanites of 4 Nephi 1:38 are a harder case than the Lamanites of every earlier book, who dwindled through the traditions of their fathers rather than by choice.

1:38.note: 'And they did not dwindle in unbelief, but they did wilfully rebel against the gospel of Christ; and they did teach their children that they should not believe.' The whole force of the sentence is the contrast between dwindling and wilfulness, which is Hebrews 10:26's distinction and is carried by its one King James adverb. The corpus has used this verse before, at Alma 39:6, where sinning against the Holy Ghost is set apart from murder as the sin for which there is no forgiveness; 4 Nephi applies the same distinction to a whole people. What makes the row more than a lexical note is the pairing with Hebrews 6:4 at 4 Nephi 1:3 — the two Hebrews apostasy passages bracket the book, and the second is the one that says why the first cannot be undone.
1:38.text: For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins,

provenance.other: “traffick” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, and two of them are the Tyre oracle, Ezekiel 28:5 and 28:18. Of the other three, one is Joseph's brothers trading in Egypt and two are commercial notices in Kings and Ezekiel 17. The Book of Mormon's 1830 spelling is 'traffic', without the King James final k. Not quoted in the New Testament, so no mediation test is available.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 28:5 states the causal chain that 4 Nephi has been narrating for twenty verses in a single sentence: 'By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches.' Traffick, then riches, then a heart lifted up. 4 Nephi runs it in the same order and splits it across the chapter — 1:23 they became exceeding rich, 1:24 they were lifted up in pride, 1:43 'proud in their hearts, because of their exceeding riches', 1:46 'did traffic in all manner of traffic'. Recover the oracle and the Nephites at the end of 4 Nephi are being described as the king of Tyre, whose sanctuaries are defiled by the iniquity of his traffick (28:18) and who is brought to ashes; which is what the next book does to them.

1:46.note: 'And gold and silver did they lay up in store in abundance, and did traffic in all manner of traffic.' The doubled construction is the Book of Mormon's own; what points at Ezekiel 28 is the rare noun plus the proposition the chapter has already stated at 1:43 in almost the oracle's words — 'proud in their hearts, because of their exceeding riches' against 'thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches'. Filed at moderate rather than high because the contact is distributed across four verses rather than concentrated in one, and because the pride-and-riches formula is standing Book of Mormon idiom covered elsewhere by exclusion; what is not standing idiom is 'traffick', which enters the corpus here.
1:46.whyNot: The two halves of the case sit in different verses, so neither alone would carry it: 1:43's clause has the proposition without the rare word and 1:46 has the rare word without the proposition. A reader who takes the pride-and-riches formula as purely internal — it is, elsewhere — is left with one uncommon noun spelled differently from its King James source, and may decline the row.
1:46.text: By thy great wisdom and by thy traffick hast thou increased thy riches, and thine heart is lifted up because of thy riches:
